attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post. He relays a revenue rumor but adopts it as his framing of the current state.

semantics.note: Keeps the valuation and revenue contrast, the 'rumored' qualifier and the hundreds-of-millions threshold. It is a present-state observation, not a forecast.

contract.note: An annual revenue scale around July 2023 is an ordinary plain reading. The contract openly flags that run rate vs realized revenue, the industry boundary and which valuations are meant are evaluator choices, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: January 2023 investor commentary says model-provider revenue was small. It gives no aggregate figure and predates the July period.

Covers one company. The earlier $200M 2023 projection is a forecast. The late-August report of >$80M/month implies OpenAI alone was near $1B annualized, which leans against the claim, but the timing relative to July and the industry aggregate are unclear.
September 2023 company deck repeats the $1.3T market forecast. This shows trillion-dollar expectations circulated, not that specific valuations depended on them.

reviews.rationale: No source in the packet gives the industry's aggregate annual revenue around July 2023. OpenAI's reported late-August run rate (~$1B annualized) suggests the scale may have exceeded hundreds of millions, but it is one company and its timing is uncertain. Valuation evidence shows only that trillion-dollar forecasts circulated. Neither condition is settled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post.

semantics.note: 'Will continue to use' is a firm forecast. The 'most likely' open-source shift is hedged and is correctly kept as a qualifier, so it is not scored.

contract.note: Scoring only the firm continued-use prediction, read as persistent group-level use, is a fair and ordinary reading. Excluding the hedged open-source component follows policy.

evidence.note: April 2024 Harvard undergraduate survey: 87.5% of respondents use generative AI. Single institution.
HEPI repeated UK undergraduate survey: generative AI use for assessments rose from just over half to 89% and then 94% by December 2025.
HEPI release confirms December 2025 fieldwork, 1,054 full-time UK undergraduates, and 'near universal' use.

reviews.rationale: Dated surveys from 2024 and repeated UK waves through December 2025 show substantial and rising undergraduate generative AI use. This meets the early-resolution rule for the firm continued-use prediction. The hedged open-source migration part is not scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words, framed as his view ('In my mind').

semantics.note: Keeps 'in my mind', 'almost everyone' and the AGI gloss. It is an evaluative observation about other people's beliefs, too vague to test.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to supply a population or a reading of 'tantamount' that Marcus did not give. Any score would depend on interpretation he did not provide.

evidence.note: US adult survey from May–July 2023 shows short AGI timelines. It does not measure whether people believed generative AI was equivalent to, or sufficient for, AGI.

reviews.rationale: The population behind 'almost everyone' is undefined, 'tantamount' is ambiguous, and the sentence mixes a claim about how widespread a belief is with Marcus's judgment that it is an error. No fair scoring condition exists, and the survey is context only.
